overview: The Alans were Iranian-speaking communities known around the Black Sea, Caspian and North Caucasus. Their history includes mobile pastoral groups, westward migrations and the medieval kingdom of Alania. These were changing communities and political arrangements across many centuries.

periods.title: Alans in ancient accounts
periods.summary: Classical writers mention Alans from the first centuries CE. Their accounts emphasize pastoral life and cavalry, while offering an external view of these communities.

periods.title: Different paths after the Hunnic invasions
periods.summary: Some Alans moved through western Europe and into North Africa. Others remained around the Black Sea and Caucasus, where settled farming communities developed.

periods.title: Kingship and Christian institutions
periods.summary: Alan rulers developed relationships with Byzantine and Georgian elites. Church patronage, titles and dress expressed political authority without making Alania a copy of Byzantium.

periods.title: Fragmentation and invasion
periods.summary: Latham-Sprinkle places the kingdom’s fragmentation before the Mongol invasions of 1238 to 1240. Rival principalities had replaced its earlier political unity.

periods.title: Communities beyond the kingdom
periods.summary: Later Alan histories include Caucasian communities, Jász settlement in Hungary and service under Mongol rulers. Political destruction did not erase every community.

items.text: Ammianus describes families moving with covered wagons, tending herds and choosing fresh pasture. Milk and meat feature in his account, and he stresses the care given to horses. This connects movement with household subsistence, although the account belongs to a Roman author describing outsiders in the fourth century.

The same passage surrounds practical details with claims about savagery and warfare. Its hostile comparisons warn against treating it as a neutral survey. In particular, its assertion that Alans did not plow cannot describe the farming settlements documented centuries later in the North Caucasus.

sections.title: Fields and the traces of ordinary work

items.text: Researchers in the Kislovodsk basin identified terraces associated with Alan communities in the first millennium CE. These differ in form and date from much older Koban agricultural terraces. Aerial photographs, geographic mapping and field investigation allow cultivated landscapes to be studied alongside settlements, rather than reducing life to graves and weapons.

The later fields largely avoided ground made infertile during earlier Koban land use. This finding shows that cultivation was shaped by the inherited condition of the landscape. It does not identify an individual inventor of terracing or establish that every Alan settlement organized farming in the same way.

Around Podkumskoe-3, a settlement associated with Alan culture in the fifth to eighth centuries, investigators found pottery, charred cereal grains and straw in soils. Together with chemical and biological soil changes, these traces identify agricultural activity beyond the settlement itself. Food production can leave evidence even where buildings do not survive.

The study identifies early medieval plowing and fertilization within roughly 500 to 600 meters of Podkumskoe-3. Farther away, the researchers instead found evidence of older Bronze Age cultivation. Distinguishing these layers prevents all nearby farmland from being assigned to one period or population.

The Met’s Alanic kaftan, cataloged around the seventh to ninth centuries, preserves fine linen, patterned silk edging and traces of fur. These materials combined a practical garment with costly decoration. The museum’s complete-looking coat includes reconstruction; the surviving original front fragment runs from neck to hem.

The coat’s silk includes animal and rosette designs within beaded roundels. The catalog relates such patterns to Iran and Central Asia without identifying a single workshop. Its back slits accommodated riding. Textile structure and garment shape reveal different aspects of making and wearing the clothing.

Harper identified Moshchevaja Balka as the coat’s probable origin by comparison with excavated textiles and correspondence with the site’s researcher. The coat entered the art market, however, and lacks a securely documented grave context. Similarity to excavated material supports an attribution, not a claim that its burial was recorded.

A renewed conservation study compared the coat with other textiles and used specialized imaging and chemical dye analysis. Digital drawings and photomicrographs helped document its construction. These methods show how fragile fragments can answer technical questions while leaving the original owner and exact burial context unresolved.

A Greek inscription at Senty Church dated 965 names the rulers David and Maria and the metropolitan Theodore. Its Byzantine architectural setting shows how Christian institutions and political authority were expressed together. Latham-Sprinkle cautions that adopting these forms does not prove replacement of the local population by Byzantine settlers.

Linguistic evidence connects Alanic with modern Ossetic. Surviving traces include an inscription in Greek letters, phrases recorded by the Byzantine writer Tzetzes, and a Jász-Latin vocabulary. These records preserve language across different settings; they do not imply that every community retained an identical identity.

ending.text: Alania fragmented into competing principalities before the Mongol invasions of 1238 to 1240. Latham-Sprinkle therefore separates the collapse of royal unity from later conquest. Communities and language outlasted the kingdom, with Alanic an ancestor of modern Ossetic. No single fall year describes the full history of the Alans.

sources.title: Vasily Abaev and Harold Bailey, Alans, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Ancient attestations, migrations, linguistic evidence and later communities. The article’s disputed Catalonia etymology and Arthurian connection are not used.

sources.title: Ammianus Marcellinus, Roman History, book 31
sources.note: Sections 2.17 to 2.25: a late Roman author’s account, including explicit hostile stereotypes. It is not treated as a timeless description of all Alans.

sources.title: Dmitry Korobov and Alexander Borisov, The origins of terraced field agriculture in the Caucasus, 2013
sources.note: Published abstract: distinct Koban and later Alan-associated terrace systems in the Kislovodsk basin; aerial photography, mapping and field investigation.

sources.title: Borisov and colleagues, Traces of ancient agriculture in the soil around archaeological sites
sources.note: Publisher’s indexed abstract and conclusion: Podkumskoe-3, fifth to eighth centuries, cereal remains and soil evidence of cultivation. Full article was not accessible.
